content: Echidnas, also referred to as spiny anteaters, are four extant mammalian species that belong to the family Tachyglossidae within the monotreme order. Alongside the platypus, they are the only surviving members of this unique group of egg-laying mammals. Despite their diet primarily consisting of ants and termites, echidnas are not closely related to true anteaters. They are native to New Guinea and Australia. The name echidna is derived from a creature in ancient Greek mythology. Echidnas are small mammals covered with coarse hair and spines. Superficially, they resemble South American anteaters and other spiny mammals such as hedgehogs and porcupines. They possess elongated, slender snouts that function as both a mouth and a nose. Their limbs are short, strong, and equipped with large claws, making them powerful diggers. Echidnas have small mouths and toothless jaws. They feed by breaking into soft logs, anthills, and similar structures, using their long, sticky tongues to capture prey. The short-beaked echidna primarily consumes ants and termites, while species of the genus Zaglossus typically feed on worms and insect larvae. Long-beaked echidnas have tiny spines on their tongues that aid in capturing their prey. Echidnas and the platypus are the only mammals that lay eggs, a characteristic of monotremes. Female echidnas lay a single soft-shelled, leathery egg approximately 22 days after mating, depositing it directly into a pouch. The egg hatches after 10 days, and the young echidna, known as a puggle, feeds on milk secreted from pores in the mother’s two milk patches (monotremes lack nipples). The puggle remains in the pouch for 45 to 55 days, during which it begins to develop spines. The mother then transfers the puggle to a nursery burrow, returning every five days to nurse it until it is weaned at around seven months of age. Male echidnas possess a four-headed penis, but only two of the heads are functional during mating, while the other two remain inactive. The functional heads alternate with each mating event. Echidnas are classified into three genera. The genus Zaglossus includes three extant species and two species known only from fossils. The genus Tachyglossus contains a single extant species, while the genus Megalibgwilia is known exclusively from fossil records. The three living species of Zaglossus are endemic to New Guinea. These species are rare and are often hunted for food. They forage in leaf litter on the forest floor, feeding on earthworms and insects. The species include: The Western Long-beaked Echidna (Zaglossus bruijni), found in highland forests. Sir David’s Long-beaked Echidna (Zaglossus attenboroughi), recently discovered and preferring even higher altitudes. The Eastern Long-beaked Echidna (Zaglossus bartoni), which has four distinct subspecies. The two fossil species of Zaglossus are: Zaglossus robustus Zaglossus hacketti The Short-beaked Echidna (Tachyglossus aculeatus) is found in southeastern New Guinea and across nearly all Australian environments, ranging from the snow-covered Australian Alps to the arid deserts of the Outback, wherever ants and termites are available. It is smaller in size compared to Zaglossus species and has longer hair.
